doc.title: Richard Wyands interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Club dates and terrible pianos
summary: Out-of-tune pianos, broken pedals, spinets, and Nat King Cole playing a spinet.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well I used to make a lot of club dates, or casuals as they were known in some areas, and the pianos were in terrible shape, terrible. They’d be out of tune, the ivory would be half on, and in fact they were so far out of tune that the musicians, the horn players, couldn’t tune up, so I would have to transpose.
You’d have to play in a different key than the rest of the band?
That’s right. Very frustrating. Or the pedals would be broken off, the sustaining pedal broken, all sorts of things, oh boy. You’re talking about dues.
Yeah. It’s almost like you want to go back and carry those drums now.
At least you know what you’re going to be dealing with.

The pianos were so bad in some of these dance halls, they had little spinets, you know what that is, that’s like just a piece of furniture, it’s not much of an instrument. I saw Nat King Cole play on a spinet. I did one of his dances like the band that played opposite him, he had his trio then, and he’s playing this little spinet. I wished I’d had a camera, a picture of that. But he was smiling too.
All the pianos that we had to play.
I would think physically it’d be really very demanding on your wrists, to get any sound out of it at all.
It is. You can’t attack it too heavily or you’ll break your arms.
